open-question.question: The orchestrator must find each task's path file in the scratch directory without the agent returning its name, and the alternatives agent's precedent derives its file name from the Short Title, so that a title holding a path separator fails the write and surfaces as a FAILED skip. Is the completion agent's path file one fixed name per run that each task's agent overwrites, or a name derived from the task title, one file per task?
open-question.recommendation: No task heading enters a file name, so a heading holding a slash or a double quote, both present among this repository's recorded headings, never ends a run with its work done and its list unwritten as the exact-title forms would; the move into processed under a unique name rides inside the orchestrator's one fixed commit call, costing no turn where an orchestrator-assigned name costs a mktemp call per dispatch, and it leaves the fixed name absent for the next task, so a missing list is detectable and every task's list stays on disk.
open-question.alternative: One fixed file name per run that every agent writes, as in the overwritten form, but the orchestrator's commit call moves the file out of the way after reading it, into a `processed` subdirectory under a name the call makes unique (for example through `mktemp` inside that subdirectory), following the alternatives pass's move-into-processed precedent and deleting nothing. The fixed name is therefore absent whenever the next agent starts, and no part of either name comes from the task title. Keeps the title out of every file name, and so free of path-separator and quoting failures, while making an agent that wrote no list show as a missing file rather than a stale one, and leaving every task's list on disk for inspection. Adds a move and a uniqueness step to the orchestrator's one commit call, and the kept files carry no readable link to the task they came from; a move that fails after the commit leaves the stale file in place for the next task, and the scheme still depends on dispatch staying sequential.

One fixed file name per run, written literally in both the agent file and the orchestrator's commit call (for example `<scratch dir>/paths`). Each task's agent overwrites it with its own recorded paths, the orchestrator reads that one literal path after every DONE, and nothing moves or renames it between tasks, so at the end of the run it holds only the last task's list. No part of the name comes from the task title. No task title ever enters a file name, so no title fails the write (2 of the 468 task headings recorded in this repository hold a `/`, and two hold a double quote), and the commit call names one constant path with no per-task substitution or shell quoting of the title; because `complete-all-tasks` dispatches one task at a time and commits before the next dispatch, overwriting never collides within a run. A previous task's list stays at the same path when an agent returns DONE without writing one, so the orchestrator cannot tell an absent file from a stale one and would re-run its guard and commit over the previous task's paths, which under same-tree parallel runs may now hold another run's live edits committed under the wrong subject (how an absent or empty file is treated belongs to a sibling question); the scratch directory keeps no per-task record, and the scheme depends on the dispatch staying sequential.

One file per task directly inside the scratch directory, named by the task's `##` heading exactly as given plus a fixed extension (for example `<scratch dir>/<Task Title>.paths`), never shortened, slugged, or escaped, as the alternatives agent names its return; the orchestrator derives the path from the heading it already holds, and a title holding a path separator fails the write, which the agent reports as `FAILED` with no directory created to make it succeed. Files are never overwritten or moved, so the directory ends the run with one list per task. Reuses the one naming rule the plugin already has for a scratch-directory return, so agent file, orchestrator call, and the dispatch-prompt invariant read alike at both dispatch sites, each task's list stays on disk under its own readable name, and a task that wrote nothing shows as a missing file rather than a stale one. A legitimate task whose heading holds a `/` cannot complete under `complete-all-tasks` and ends the run on a `FAILED` after doing its work, since the list is written at the end of the task; and the orchestrator's commit call must carry the heading inside a quoted path, where a title's double quote, `$`, or backtick needs the same care the commit subject already does.

One directory per task inside the scratch directory, named by the task's `##` heading exactly as given (`<scratch dir>/<Task Title>/`), holding the path list under a fixed file name, the layout the draft's second milestone describes for the commit message and the recorded paths together; the agent creates the directory and writes the list into it, a title holding a path separator is stated to fail as a `FAILED`, and nothing is overwritten or moved. Lands the layout the draft's next milestone already plans, so adding the commit-message file there adds one file beside the list rather than renaming this milestone's return, while keeping per-task records and making a missing list detectable. Asks the agent for a directory creation as well as a write for one file this milestone, and a separator in the title no longer fails on its own (a parent-creating `mkdir` or write tool builds nested directories and succeeds), so the failure holds only by the agent obeying a stated rule; it carries the exact-title form's quoting cost and its `FAILED` for headings holding a `/`.

One file per task named by a fixed transform of the task's `##` heading (for example path separators and shell-special characters replaced, the rest kept) plus a fixed extension, the transform stated once and applied identically by the agent when writing and by the orchestrator when reading; no title fails the write, and nothing is overwritten or moved. Every task can complete whatever its heading holds, while keeping one readable, detectable file per task and keeping shell-special characters out of the path the commit call quotes. The transform must be stated so both runners apply it identically, and a drift between the agent file and the orchestrator silently loses a task's list; two headings that differ only in replaced characters map to one name although the task-list tool keeps them distinct, and it departs from the alternatives agent's explicit never-slug rule, giving the plugin two naming rules for scratch-directory returns.

The orchestrator chooses each task's file name itself, free of the title (for example the task's ordinal in the run), and passes it to the agent as one more fixed line in the dispatch prompt (or passes the full file path in place of the bare scratch directory); the agent writes exactly the path it was given, and nothing is overwritten or moved. No title character can break the name or the commit call's quoting, each task still gets its own file so a missing list is detectable, and the agent applies no naming rule of its own. Adds a per-dispatch value the orchestrator must generate and hold across loop iterations, and grows the two-line prompt fence (and the Antigravity on-demand test's prompt helper) beyond the goal's scratch-directory line, against the dispatch-prompt rule's preference for the smallest prompt; the kept files carry no readable link to their task.

open-question.question: The commit tool prints a fixed result when its dirty-own-path guard finds nothing to commit, while its sibling tools signal every refusal with one Error: line on stderr and a non-zero exit, and every fixed call chains the tool behind && and echoes its landed-commit marker after a successful exit. Does the tool's no-op exit 0, as a success whose fixed line the calling runner reads, or exit non-zero like a refusal, so a chained call ends there and echoes no marker?

recommendation.option: Exit 0, call gates marker on output

open-question.recommendation: A no-op is a success, as every sibling mutator's no-op already exits 0, and the by-reference skills and the recommendation pass's routine ordering no-op must not end a call on a status a runner reads as failure; keeping the tool to one output contract, nothing on success and its fixed line on a no-op, puts the marker gate in each fixed call as one capture and test, rather than giving the tool an optional marker argument or a per-call flag that branches its contract.

alternative.id: Exit 0, call gates marker on output

open-question.alternative: The no-op exits 0. The tool prints its fixed no-op line on stdout and prints nothing when a commit lands, which keeps the siblings' rule that a mutator prints nothing on success. Refusals and a git failure after the last retry keep exit 1 with one Error: line on stderr. Each of the seven fixed calls captures the tool's stdout and echoes its own landed-commit marker only when that capture is empty, so the marker no longer rides a bare &&. The eleven skills that follow the procedure by reference read the printed line directly to choose their no-op line. A no-op is a clean success everywhere, as `strip` and `sort` already treat theirs. Skills such as `goto-next-milestone`, `finish-current-milestone`, `init-milestone-base-workflow`, and a no-op review pass, where the no-op is routine, never see a non-zero exit for a normal outcome. Chains that must keep going past a no-op keep going unchanged: the recommendation pass's `fi && sort`, the answer sweep's `|| stopped at`, and the alternatives loop's failed-commit report. Every fixed call grows a capture and a test on the tool's text in place of today's plain `&& echo`. That is more shell for runners to copy exactly and for the fixed-call tests to extract. It also makes a call's correctness depend on the tool's success output staying empty.

The no-op exits 0 and prints the tool's fixed no-op line on stdout. The tool takes an optional argument carrying the caller's landed-commit marker text, such as `completion commit landed`, and prints it itself only when the commit lands. Each fixed call passes its marker through that argument and drops its trailing `&& echo`. The by-reference skills pass none and read the no-op line. Refusals and git failures keep exit 1 with an Error: line. A no-op is success, so no chain needs to tell it apart from a failure. Each fixed call gets shorter instead of longer, because the guard, the commit, and the marker all live in one tested process, and the recommendation pass can still tell its annotation marker from its ordering marker. The tool prints caller-supplied text as its own output, a contract no sibling tool has. It ties the markers, which each skill's status line reads, to a tool argument rather than a visible echo in the skill's fence. Every fixed call's marker wording also moves into an argument, so the fixed-call tests and any reader looking for the marker line must look inside the command.

By default the no-op exits 0 and prints the tool's fixed no-op line on stdout. A flag on the command makes the no-op exit non-zero instead, with the same line, for callers that want it. The fixed calls that chain `&& echo marker` pass the flag, so the marker stays honest with no output test. The by-reference skills and any chain that must run on past a no-op omit it. Refusals and git failures keep exit 1 with an Error: line. Each caller gets the exit behaviour that fits it without adding shell logic. The chained calls keep today's `&& echo` shape, and the skills where a no-op is routine see a clean exit. The tool has two exit contracts for one condition, and every call site has to pick one correctly. A missing or misplaced flag either echoes a false landed marker or stops a chain on a harmless no-op, and nothing but review catches it. The flag also doubles the no-op cases the tool's tests must pin.

The no-op exits non-zero with an exit code reserved for it, distinct from the refusal code 1 and argparse's usage code 2. It prints the tool's fixed no-op line on stdout, not as an Error: line. Every fixed call keeps `&& echo marker`, which correctly echoes nothing on a no-op. Where a no-op must not end the chain, the call tests for that one code, for example `|| [ $? -eq <code> ]`, so that a no-op continues while a refusal or a git failure still stops. That covers the recommendation pass's `&& sort`, the answer sweep's `stopped at` branch, and the alternatives loop's failed-commit report. The by-reference skills tell the no-op from a failure by the code and the stdout line, never by an error's wording. The marker stays honest with no change to the `&& echo` idiom. A shell can still tell a no-op from a refusal by code alone, so no runner or call classifies text. The draft's `gate` query already uses a non-zero exit with a stdout print for a non-error outcome. The by-reference skills, where a no-op is routine, see a non-zero exit for a normal outcome. A runner or a headless harness may read that as a failure and try to fix it. It also breaks the siblings' pattern that only a refusal exits non-zero. Each chain that must run past a no-op needs a code test, and the code becomes one more contract that has to stay fixed across versions.

The no-op is reported exactly like every other refusal: exit 1 with one fixed Error: line on stderr, sharing its exit code with a git failure after the last retry. Every fixed call keeps `&& echo marker` and ends its chain at a no-op. This is harmless wherever the preceding tool write always changes a path (`remove`, `embed`, `move`, `insert`) or the commit is the call's last step, as with the recommendation pass's ordering commit. The by-reference skills choose their no-op line from the Error: line's fixed text. It needs a single exit contract, the one every sibling tool already uses, so there is nothing new to learn, test, or keep fixed. The chained calls keep their present shape, with no capture, flag, or code test. A no-op and a git failure share one exit code, so any runner that must react differently to them has to classify the Error: line's wording, which the fixed-line convention otherwise forbids. That applies to the by-reference skills, whose no-op is a clean stop with its own fixed line. Any chain that could hit a no-op with work still after it stops there. The routine no-op of `goto-next-milestone` or `finish-current-milestone` would also surface as an error.

open-question.question: Today a DONE with nothing staged is a no-op the whole-index guard absorbs; once the change set travels as a file, an absent or empty file after DONE is a distinct condition, an agent that completed the task but wrote no path list, which a guard on the file's paths cannot tell from a task that changed nothing. When an agent returns DONE and its path file is absent or empty, does the orchestrator take the task as having produced no committable change, or stop the run on a fixed stop line of its own?
open-question.recommendation: With the agent listing the two task files every DONE's file holds at least the two paths the move just changed, so an absent or empty file is a broken return contract and never a change-free task; stopping keeps the move and the edits out of a later task's commit, and the fixed-line convention gives the check that ended the run its own identifier-free line rather than the no-status line, which misdescribes a DONE.
open-question.alternative: An absent and an empty path file are both a stop condition: the orchestrator commits nothing, ends the run, and prints a new fixed identifier-free stop line of its own (one new row in the fixed-lines table and its test), with the task name and which of absent or empty it found on the lines below. The tree is left as the agent left it, resumable, with the move and the edits uncommitted. A broken return contract is never absorbed silently: the operator or a harness sees a distinct, matchable line naming exactly this condition, and nothing is committed under a change set the orchestrator cannot vouch for. A task that legitimately changed nothing beyond the task list stops a headless run if an empty file is how it reports that, which depends on whether the agent's file lists the two task files (then an empty file is never legitimate) or the orchestrator adds them (then it can be), a sibling's axis; it also adds a fixed line, a table row, and a test.

An absent and an empty path file after DONE are both taken as a task that produced no committable change: the orchestrator commits nothing for that task, creates no empty commit, goes on to the next task, and counts the task toward the run's committed-nothing no-op line exactly as today's whole-index guard does for a DONE with nothing staged. No new console line is added. A long headless run is never interrupted by a return-file slip, and the orchestrator keeps today's semantics for a DONE that brought nothing to commit, so neither the fixed-lines table nor any harness matching it changes. A task the agent did complete, moving its section in TASKS_TODO.md and TASKS_DONE.md and editing project files, is left uncommitted with nothing reported; because every later commit is pathspec-bound, the stranded project edits never ride into a commit and stay dirty, while the moved task files ride into the next task's Task-completion: commit (wherever the task files are named, a sibling's axis) and misattribute the move, or stay dirty after the last task.

An absent and an empty path file are both taken as a task with no project change, but the orchestrator still commits the two task files it can name from the milestone directory it holds, TASKS_TODO.md and TASKS_DONE.md, under Task-completion: <Task Title>, and goes on to the next task. No stop and no new console line; any project edits the agent made but did not list stay uncommitted in the tree. The task's completion is always recorded in its own commit, so the move never leaks into the next task's commit, and the run continues uninterrupted for a task that genuinely touched only the task list. A missing list silently splits a task's change set: its section lands as done in history while its project edits stay dirty and unattributed, exactly the change silently left out of a commit the path file exists to prevent; a later task's agent may then take them up under the resumption rule as earlier or another run's work.

An absent and an empty path file are both a stop, reported through the existing no-status condition: a DONE without a usable path file is treated as a return with no usable status, so the run stops on the existing line `Task run stopped — a task agent returned no status.` with the task name and what was missing below it, commits nothing, and leaves the tree resumable. No new fixed line is added; the condition's test is widened from the message alone to the message plus its file. The failure is caught and stops the run without growing the fixed-lines contract, so a harness already matching the no-status stop handles the new case with no change. The line misdescribes the case, since the agent did return DONE and the task's move is already in the tree, and one line now covers two checks, against the convention that each stop condition opens with a line of its own; a harness or operator reading it as a model failure looks in the wrong place.

The two cases are told apart: the agent always writes the path file, empty when it changed nothing beyond the task list, so an absent file is a breach of its return contract and stops the run on a new fixed stop line of its own (task name below, nothing committed, tree resumable), while an empty file is a task with no project change and the orchestrator commits only the two task files it names from the milestone directory, then continues. A contract breach and a genuinely change-free task get different, correct handling: the breach is never absorbed, and a verification-only or documentation-free task neither stops a headless run nor leaves its move uncommitted. It is coherent only if the orchestrator rather than the agent supplies the task files (if the agent lists them, an empty file is as much a breach as an absent one), a sibling's axis; and an agent that wrote the file but forgot to record its edits still passes as change-free, its edits left dirty, while the agent contract gains the always-write rule and the fixed-lines table one row.

The two cases are told apart as in the split above: the agent always writes the path file, an empty file commits only the two task files the orchestrator names from the milestone directory and the run continues, and an absent file stops the run, but through the existing no-status condition and its line `Task run stopped — a task agent returned no status.` rather than a new one, the missing file below it, nothing committed, tree resumable. It keeps the split's correct handling of a change-free task while adding no fixed line, since a DONE whose promised file never appeared is reported as the incomplete return it is. It shares the split's dependence on the orchestrator supplying the task files (a sibling's axis) and its blindness to an empty file that omits real edits, and the reused line still says no status where the agent said DONE, one line standing for two checks.

open-question.question: The orchestrator's no-op line `Task run committed nothing — no task staged a change.` names staging, which the agent no longer does, and a fixed line is a contract harnesses match across versions, changing only together with its row in the fixed-lines table. Does the line keep its wording unchanged, or is it reworded to stop naming the retired mechanism?
open-question.recommendation: With the task files always in the agent's file and a missing or empty file a stop, every DONE the orchestrator commits from carries the two paths the move just changed, so a run that commits nothing cannot occur and the line would promise harnesses an outcome that never happens; retiring it with its table row ends the stale staging wording without spending a whole-line contract change on a rewording.
open-question.alternative: The committed-nothing condition, its fixed line, and its row in the fixed-lines table are removed. A run whose tasks all returned `DONE` always ends on `All tasks completed.`, and step 2c's per-task guard either stays as a silent skip or goes with the line. `tests/test_fixed_console_lines.py` needs no change of its own, because it checks only the rows the table lists. It removes a line describing a condition the new commit call cannot reach. Every `DONE` follows a successful `move`, which changes `TASKS_TODO.md` and `TASKS_DONE.md`, and those files reach the commit one way or another, so a whole run with nothing committed cannot happen. The plugin then stops promising harnesses an outcome that never occurs, and the stale wording question goes away with it. A harness matching the line loses it with no replacement, and an outcome that was listed simply disappears from the contract. Whether the condition is truly unreachable depends on the sibling questions on whether the task files reach the commit through the path file or from the orchestrator's own directory, and on what a missing or empty path file after `DONE` means. If the line is retired and a reachable case is left, the run would print the success line over a run that committed nothing.

The no-op line stays byte-for-byte `Task run committed nothing — no task staged a change.`, in `core/skills/complete-all-tasks/SKILL.md` and in its row of `docs/skill-reference.md`'s `## Fixed console lines` table alike. Only the prose around it changes: the sentence introducing the line, and the step-2c guard it summarizes, are rewritten for the commit-from-file call, while the printed line itself still says "staged". No harness matching the line across versions breaks, and nothing in the fixed-lines table, `tests/test_fixed_console_lines.py`, or any host tree needs touching for it. That keeps the contract the table exists to provide, under which a line changes only when it has to. The line names a mechanism the milestone retires. Once the agent stops staging, "no task staged a change" describes nothing that happens in the run. A reader or harness author would take it at face value, and it would disagree with the reworded `docs/workflow.md`, `docs/skill-reference.md`, and the committing invariant, which will no longer say anything is staged by the agent.

The line keeps its opening clause `Task run committed nothing —` and only the reason after the dash is reworded to name no git or hand-off mechanism, for example `Task run committed nothing — no task changed a file.` The reworded line replaces the old one in `complete-all-tasks` and in its fixed-lines table row in the same change, and `tests/test_fixed_console_lines.py` then checks the new text in every host tree. The line stops naming the retired mechanism and names none to replace it, so it survives the draft's later milestones changing how a change set travels again. Keeping the prefix lets a harness that matches on the clause before the dash keep working. This matches the shape of sibling no-op lines such as `complete-task`'s `No task completed — no file changed.` Any harness matching the whole line, which is the form the table and the test define, breaks on upgrade and has to update its match. A one-time contract change is spent on wording alone, for a condition that is rarely if ever reached, because a successful move always changes the two task files.

The line is reworded to name the mechanism that replaces staging: the paths each agent writes to its file in the run's scratch directory. An example is `Task run committed nothing — no task recorded a changed path.` It is changed together with its fixed-lines table row and checked by `tests/test_fixed_console_lines.py` as in any rewording. It says exactly what the orchestrator's guard checks under the new design, so the line keeps describing the run's real mechanism the way the old one did when it was written. A reader who sees it knows to look at the agents' path files, not at the index. It breaks whole-line harness matches just as any rewording does, and it ties the line to a mechanism again, so a later change to how the change set travels would force another rewording. Its accuracy also depends on the sibling questions on whether the path file lists the task files and on how a missing or empty path file is handled. If a missing file is treated as no committable change, "recorded" no longer holds for that case.
